content: The BPaL regimen, which includes bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, is a critical treatment option for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), particularly in cases with additional fluoroquinolone resistance. However, its implementation requires significant enhancement in many countries due to the increasing use of bedaquiline and linezolid, even in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens, and the inclusion of new drugs like pretomanid. Baseline drug susceptibility testing (DST) is essential to confirm eligibility for the BPaL regimen, making the establishment and strengthening of DST services a vital consideration for implementation. For patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB, the MTBDRsl assay is recommended as the initial test to detect resistance to fluoroquinolones and, if necessary, second-line injectable drugs, rather than relying on culture and phenotypic DST. If DST for bedaquiline or linezolid is available, it is highly desirable to perform these tests at baseline. DST for pretomanid is still under development. In settings where laboratory capacity for fluoroquinolone DST is unavailable, conducting operational research on the BPaL regimen will be challenging. Patients with strains resistant to any of the drugs in the BPaL regimen should be started on a longer MDR-TB regimen. Improving access to DST for all components of the BPaL regimen is necessary. This includes ensuring the availability of drug powders and data on the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) distribution of all circulating Mycobacterium tuberculosis lineages globally. In the Nix-TB study, all medications were administered with food, and study medications were supervised according to local site practices to support patient adherence. Preventing treatment interruptions is crucial to improving treatment success rates. Tailored measures to support patient adherence, such as communityor home-based directly observed therapy (DOT) by trained supporters, social support, and digital health interventions, are essential to retain patients on treatment and ensure favorable outcomes. Treatment response is monitored through monthly sputum smear microscopy and culture, similar to the schedule used for longer MDR-TB regimens. Updated definitions for treatment outcomes are awaited, but current reporting frameworks for shorter MDR-TB regimens align with those for longer regimens. Treatment must be closely monitored to ensure optimal drug effectiveness and safety and to detect emerging drug resistance. Given the novelty of the BPaL regimen, which includes a new drug and is implemented under operational research conditions, post-treatment follow-up is critical to ensure no relapse occurs. In the Nix-TB study, post-treatment monitoring was conducted monthly for the first three months, followed by three-month intervals, for a total of 24 months. Due to the high rate of adverse events observed in the Nix-TB study, active safety monitoring is essential for patients receiving the BPaL regimen. Baseline and ongoing clinical and laboratory testing should be conducted, including assessments for fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, liver tenderness, and hepatomegaly, as well as laboratory tests for liver enzymes, complete blood count, and serum electrolytes. Clinicians should also perform an ECG before initiating treatment. The Nix-TB study employed a comprehensive baseline clinical assessment, followed by weekly monitoring until week 20, and then every 4–6 weeks thereafter, depending on the treatment duration (6 or 9 months). Detailed schedules for baseline and follow-up monitoring, including post-treatment, should be developed for any BPaL operational research protocol, with standardized measures for recording adverse events. The WHO framework for active drug safety monitoring and management (aDSM) should be applied to all MDR-TB regimens to ensure appropriate action and prompt responses to adverse events, alongside monitoring for treatment outcomes and early detection of treatment failure. Additional evidence on adverse events is needed to build the safety evidence base for the BPaL regimen in diverse settings. Monitoring changes in linezolid dosing and duration, when necessary, is particularly important to inform future evidence on the regimen's wider use and linezolid tolerability. Linezolid pharmacokinetics in MDR-TB patients with fluoroquinolone resistance are nonlinear, and individual linezolid concentration times are the best predictors of toxicity. Higher toxicity rates were observed at higher total daily doses, with similar rates for twice-daily (BID) and once-daily (QD) dosing schedules. Data modeling suggests that anemia can be managed by closely monitoring hemoglobin changes during the first four weeks of treatment. A hemoglobin decrease of more than 10% from baseline should prompt a reduction in the linezolid dose, as hemoglobin levels recover well after dose reductions. Peripheral neuropathy and optic neuritis should also be closely monitored. Thrombocytopenia was not a major concern at high linezolid doses for MDR-TB patients with fluoroquinolone resistance. Adverse events related to pretomanid, particularly potential safety signals regarding male infertility observed in animal models, require further investigation. Monitoring infertility in programmatic settings poses challenges. Additional human sperm studies recommended by the US FDA will be conducted by the TB Alliance, but these data were unavailable for consideration at the time of the meeting. Infertility is a serious issue affecting patients and their families, and further research is needed to evaluate the balance of desirable and undesirable effects before deciding on the global programmatic implementation of the BPaL regimen. A monitoring schedule should be established and applied to all patients receiving the BPaL regimen. This should include baseline, during-treatment, and post-treatment evaluations, encompassing clinical assessments, bacteriological and laboratory tests, radiology, and ECG examinations. The baseline visit marks the start of BPaL treatment, and the monitoring schedule should consider specific situations, such as elderly patients, those with HIV, hepatitis, or diabetes, and those with hepatic or renal impairment. Active pharmacovigilance and proper management of adverse events are essential, as is the prevention of complications from drug–drug interactions. National tuberculosis programs (NTPs) should actively monitor drug safety, report adverse events to the responsible drug safety authority, and inform national and global policy. Safe management of adverse events may require dose reduction or discontinuation of component drugs. However, the BPaL regimen has been studied as a standardized treatment course, and early discontinuation or replacement of any component drug may result in poor outcomes. In cases where the regimen must be discontinued, patients should be evaluated and switched to an individualized longer regimen based on WHO guidelines. Common reasons for discontinuation include intolerable toxicity, treatment failure, resistance to BPaL drugs, or pregnancy during treatment. If bedaquiline or pretomanid must be discontinued, the entire regimen should be stopped. If linezolid is permanently discontinued within the first four weeks of treatment, the regimen should also be discontinued. Temporary cessation of linezolid or the full regimen is allowed for suspected drug-related toxicity, with reintroduction possible after no more than 35 consecutive days of cessation. If linezolid is permanently discontinued later in the regimen, clinicians should assess the patient and consider continuing bedaquiline and pretomanid for the remainder of the regimen. Elective partial lung resection surgery, such as lobectomy or wedge resection, may be considered as an adjunct to chemotherapy for MDR/RR-TB and XDR-TB patients, particularly in cases with intractable pathology or high bacterial loads. This approach requires skilled thoracic surgeons and excellent postoperative care. However, radical pneumonectomy is not recommended due to a lack of statistically significant benefit.
